Baroque is the exuberant artistic and architectural style that emerged in late 16th-century Europe, particularly in Catholic regions responding to the Counter-Reformation. The style is characterized by dramatic emotion, dynamic composition, rich ornamentation, and theatrical use of light and shadow. It was deliberately designed to move the viewer spiritually and emotionally. The Baroque period spans roughly 1600 to 1750, originating in Rome at the height of the Counter-Reformation and spreading throughout Catholic Europe and its colonial territories. The style emerged partly as a reaction against the Protestant Reformation's critique of Catholic visual devotion. Baroque art used sensory richness and emotional intensity to justify the religious use of images and artistic beauty. Major artists include Gian Lorenzo Bernini, the sculptor and architect, Caravaggio, who pioneered dramatic lighting called chiaroscuro, Peter Paul Rubens, and Francesco Borromini, the architect. Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome became the quintessential expression of Baroque grandeur, with its colonnade, plaza, and interior decoration under Bernini exemplifying the style's monumentality. Baroque architecture features curved facades, complex geometries, elaborate sculptural decoration, and dramatic plays of light through windows and mirrors. In painting, artists employed chiaroscuro, foreshortening, diagonal compositions, and dynamic gestures to convey spiritual ecstasy and divine presence. Baroque music, composed by Bach, Handel, and Vivaldi, paralleled the visual arts in complexity, ornamentation, and emotional intensity.
